Our tiffin start-up lasted fourteen months. My co-founder Pema and I started it at twenty-four: home-style lunches for office workers in Pune, cooked by women from our neighbourhood.
The first three months were magic. We had two hundred customers from a word-of-mouth list and a spreadsheet. An investor gave us a small amount after one meeting. We hired, bought a van, rented a kitchen.
Then offices went hybrid. Orders halved in six weeks. We kept spending as if they'd come back. I stopped sleeping. My mother kept asking, "Beta, are you eating?"
In month thirteen, Pema said it first: "We have to shut it down properly." We paid every cook, returned what we could, and wrote to each customer.
I'm Sahil. It hurt like a breakup. But I learned more in those fourteen months than in college: test before you spend, watch your cash every week, and end honestly.

qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when orders halved?
qa.a: Sahil felt anxious and overwhelmed, to the point of not sleeping.

qa.q: What lessons from Sahil's failure could help another founder?
qa.a: Test demand before spending, track cash weekly, and when it's over, shut down honestly by paying people and telling customers.

qa.q: How might the cooks have felt about the way the venture ended?
qa.a: The cooks were probably sad to lose the work but respected being paid in full and told honestly.

grounding: Shows a young founder taking a venture from idea to customers and learning from its shutdown.

Tanvir writing. Today Kashish and I told our team of six that the app is shutting down. Two years. Three pivots. No more money.

In Johannesburg, Zanele was preparing the quarterly report for a big retail client. The campaign had flopped: sales barely moved.
Her boss, Thabo, leaned over her desk. "Show the clicks, not the sales. Make it look like a success. They'll renew."
Zanele's stomach tightened. The clicks had come mostly from bots, which she'd flagged last month.
She took a breath. "If they find out later, we lose them and our name. Can I show what worked, what didn't, and what we'll change? I think honesty is how we keep them."
Thabo sighed. "And if they leave?"
"Then they leave trusting us. And they might come back."
He tapped the desk. "Show me both versions by five."
She did. He chose hers, with a line added about a new approach. The client didn't renew for six months. Then they came back with a smaller project.

Week 1: Joseph and his wife had just moved into their flat in Kochi. His cousin Mohit's family started dropping in without warning, three evenings in a row, expecting dinner. Joseph's wife said nothing, but her jaw tightened each time.
Week 2: Joseph noticed he was dreading the doorbell. He talked to his wife. "I love Mohit. But we need our evenings." They agreed Joseph would say it, since it was his family.
Week 3: On the phone, Joseph said, "Mohit, we'd love to have you over. But can you call before coming? And let's fix Sunday lunches, every other week?"
Mohit was quiet, then laughed awkwardly. "Our mother always said family doesn't need to call."
"I know. But we're new at this."
The next Sunday lunch, Mohit brought payasam and called ahead. Joseph's wife smiled properly for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What did Mohit bring to the Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Payasam.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel by the second week?
qa.a: Joseph felt dread and tension, not wanting the doorbell to ring.

qa.q: Why did it help that Joseph set the boundary himself?
qa.a: Since it was his family, hearing it from him felt less like rejection from an outsider, and he could offer a warm alternative.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when Joseph asked him to call first?
qa.a: Mohit probably felt a bit hurt and awkward, since his mother taught that family doesn't need to call, but he accepted.

grounding: Illustrates a young man holding a boundary with relatives over several weeks while keeping the relationship warm.

"How long have you been in Hyderabad now?" Jahnavi asked, passing the samosa plate.
"Eight months," Jasleen said. "And I still don't have anyone I'd call at 2 a.m."
"You have me."
"You've been here three weeks!"
Jahnavi laughed. "Fair. So what have you tried?"
"Office friends. We only talk about work. A dance class, but I kept missing it."
"That's the thing. Friendships need showing up. Same place, same time, again and again."
"Like what?"
"My cousin joined a Saturday running group near the lake. Same twenty people every week. By month three, they were helping each other move flats."
Jasleen thought. "And if I miss a week?"
"Then you text someone from the group. You build it on being reliable."
"Okay. Saturday. You're coming too."

qa.q: How long has Jasleen been in Hyderabad?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel about having no one to call at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Jasleen feels lonely and a little discouraged, despite trying office friends and a dance class.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi suggest about building community, and why does it work?
qa.a: Showing up at the same place and time again and again, because trust grows from being reliable.

qa.q: If you were Jahnavi, what would you want from agreeing to go on Saturday?
qa.a: You might want a new friend and a group too, since Jahnavi is even newer to the city.

grounding: Illustrates young adults discussing how reliable, repeated contact builds community and trusted networks.

passage:
When I moved to Delhi at twenty-three for my first job, I didn't know a single person. I'm Lalremsiami, from Aizawl, and the city felt enormous.
For the first year I said yes to everything, parties, groups, events, and ended up with a hundred contacts and no real friends.
Then Bhupen, a senior at work, gave me advice I still use. "Pick a few people and be reliable to them. Remember their mother's surgery. Turn up when they move house. Ask about the thing they told you last month."
So I narrowed down. A monthly potluck with five people from the northeast. A mentor, Bhupen himself, whom I met every six weeks with real questions. A neighbourhood library where I volunteered on Saturdays.
Two years later, when I was ill with dengue, four people brought food. Bhupen called my manager. I had a network, not a contact list.

qa.q: How many people brought food when Lalremsiami was ill?
qa.a: Four people.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel during the first year in Delhi?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt lost in the huge city and still lonely, despite a hundred contacts.

qa.q: What changed Lalremsiami's approach to building a network, and why did it work?
qa.a: Choosing a few people and being reliable to them, with regular potlucks, a mentor and volunteering, built real trust over time.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel when he calls Lalremsiami's manager?
qa.a: Bhupen probably feels protective and glad that the relationship he encouraged is now one of real care.

grounding: Shows a young adult investing in reliable friendships, a mentor and community ties in a new city.

Resident welfare association note. Santosh, secretary.
Pema, 24, moved into Block C last year and at first kept to himself. In March he came to a meeting to complain about the broken streetlight. He stayed to help write the letter to the municipal office.
Since then, he's become one of our most dependable members. He set up a phone tree for elderly residents living alone, so each has two neighbours who check on them. He helps Mrs D'Souza with her grocery app, and he fixed the Sharmas' router.
He told me he'd felt lonely when he arrived. Now, he said, when his scooter broke down last month, three neighbours offered lifts before he'd asked.
I've asked him to join the committee. He hesitated; he thinks he's too young. I told him trust isn't about age. It's about who shows up.

qa.a: Pema felt lonely when he first moved into Block C.

Asif's father died in October, suddenly, in their small town near Aligarh. Asif was twenty-five, the eldest son, and suddenly in charge of the family shop, the paperwork and his grieving mother.
For weeks he opened the shop at dawn and closed at night and didn't let himself feel anything. Then one afternoon, a customer asked for "the blue notebooks your father used to keep," and Asif had to go into the back room and sit on a sack of rice until his breathing slowed.
Bhavna, who ran the stationery shop next door, came in with tea. She'd lost her own father two years earlier. "You don't have to be strong every minute," she said.
After that, Asif made small changes. He closed the shop on Friday afternoons to sit with his mother. He asked his cousin to help with the accounts. He began reading his father's old notebooks at night, one page at a time.

qa.q: What did the customer ask Asif for?
qa.a: "The blue notebooks your father used to keep."

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he sat on the sack of rice?
qa.a: Asif was overwhelmed by grief he had been holding back, struggling to breathe calmly.

qa.q: Which of Asif's changes helped him rebuild after the loss?
qa.a: Closing on Friday afternoons for his mother, sharing the accounts and reading his father's notebooks gave him support, rest and a way to grieve.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt bringing Asif tea?
qa.a: Bhavna probably felt compassion and a painful recognition, having lost her own father two years earlier. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young adult grieving a sudden loss and rebuilding routine, support and meaning.

passage:
Layla was twenty-six and teaching primary school in Beirut when she was diagnosed with a serious illness that meant months of treatment. She had to stop working. Her world shrank to hospital corridors and her flat.
Her friend Tuan, who'd moved there for work, came on Tuesdays. At first Layla didn't want visitors. She felt like a patient, not a person.
One Tuesday he asked, "What do you miss most?" She said, "Being useful. My class."
So they found small ways. She recorded short stories for her pupils on her phone, and their teacher played them in class. On good days she and Tuan walked to the corner bakery. She joined an online group for young adults in treatment and found people who laughed at the same terrible hospital food.
Treatment was still hard. But her days had shape again, and a reason.

qa.q: What did Layla record for her pupils?
qa.a: Short stories on her phone.

qa.q: How did Layla feel at first when Tuan visited?
qa.a: Layla felt low and frustrated, reduced to a patient rather than a person, and didn't want visitors.

qa.q: What helped Layla rebuild meaning during treatment?
qa.a: Finding ways to still be useful, like the stories for her class, plus small outings and an online group of people in similar situations.

qa.q: How might Layla's pupils feel hearing her recorded stories?
qa.a: The pupils probably feel happy and connected to their teacher, even while she's away.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing serious illness and rebuilding routine, support and meaning.

passage:
Two years after the flood that destroyed their home in a small town in Assam, Parveen still couldn't sleep when it rained hard. She'd sit up with the lights on, listening to the water, her whole body tight. In daytime she was fine, working at the school office. She told herself it was silly.
Then the monsoon came again, and one night she couldn't stop shaking. The next morning she went to the community health centre, where Ishita, a counsellor, ran a group for flood survivors.
In the group, Parveen heard others describe the same thing: rain, fear, the night the water came. She wasn't strange. Ishita taught them grounding: naming five things they could see, feeling their feet on the floor. She met Parveen alone every two weeks too.
This monsoon, Parveen still woke up during storms. But she could name the five things, breathe, and go back to sleep.

qa.q: Where did Ishita run the group for flood survivors?
qa.a: At the community health centre.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel during heavy rain at night?
qa.a: Parveen felt frightened and tense, sitting up with the lights on, unable to sleep.

qa.q: Which kinds of support helped Parveen heal, and why?
qa.a: The survivors' group showed she wasn't alone, and grounding techniques plus individual sessions gave her ways to calm her body.

qa.q: How might other group members have felt hearing Parveen's story?
qa.a: They probably felt understood and less alone, recognising their own fears in hers.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising lingering effects of a disaster and using therapy and community to heal.

Three months after a robbery at the pharmacy where he worked in Bogotá, Mateo still jumped every time the shop door opened. He'd been at the till when two men came in with a knife. Nobody was hurt. He kept saying that, as if it meant he shouldn't feel anything.
His colleague Kofi noticed him checking the door, over and over, and snapping at customers who came in quickly.
One evening, closing up, Kofi said, "I was robbed at my last job in Accra. I didn't sleep properly for months. The company counsellor helped me."
Mateo stared at him. "You too?"
"Me too."
The next day Mateo called the employee support line and booked sessions. He also asked the manager to move him away from the till for a few weeks. Healing was slow. But he started noticing the door less, and laughing more.

qa.q: Where had Mateo been standing during the robbery?
qa.a: At the till.

qa.q: What does Mateo's jumping at the door suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Mateo was still frightened and on edge, even months later, despite saying nobody was hurt.

qa.q: Which of Mateo's steps helped him begin to heal?
qa.a: Calling the employee support line for counselling and asking to be moved from the till for a while.

qa.q: How might Kofi have felt sharing his own robbery story?
qa.a: Kofi probably felt a little exposed but caring, wanting Mateo to know he wasn't weak or alone.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult recognising lingering effects of a robbery and seeking counselling and workplace support.
